questions.question: Define scarcity, separate it from a shortage, and explain why even great wealth offers no escape from it.
questions.expected_answer: Scarcity is the permanent, universal condition in which resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants; it cannot be closed because wants grow with means and refill as they are met. A shortage is a temporary market situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price — ended by price adjustment or fresh supply, like cooking oil returning after a supply scare. A wealthy family meets almost no shortages yet still lives under scarcity: its wants move upmarket, and time stays scarce for everyone — no fortune buys a twenty-fifth hour. Scarcity therefore forces ranking: which want is met now, which waits, which never.

questions.question: Define opportunity cost with its two answer disciplines, and apply it at household, business and state level.
questions.expected_answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up — the runner-up only, never everything forgone. Discipline one: state it in real terms — the alternative itself, such as 'one month's gym membership', never in rands, since the money was spent either way. Discipline two: rank the alternatives first, then name the runner-up. Household: the Sunday car-wash shift's true cost is the afternoon of maths revision forgone. Business: Lerato's R7 500 fridge costs the mark-up her extra stock would have earned. State: two billion rand on an interchange is two billion withdrawn from clinics and school maintenance — every budget debate is an opportunity-cost argument. Even free things cost the time they take.

questions.question: Name the three questions every economy must answer, match the three systems to who answers them, and weigh the brickworks scenario in both columns.
questions.expected_answer: What to produce (the basket), how to produce (labour- versus capital-intensive — heavy in a high-unemployment country), and for whom (distribution — the most political). Market economies let prices answer; planned economies let the state answer; mixed economies — South Africa emphatically included — let markets answer most questions while the state corrects, redistributes and provides. The scenario: promotion column — jobs, wages, taxes funding rights; violation column — smoke in the valley's lungs and ash in the stream, an externality no price collected, threatening sustainability. Remedies: enforce regulation, make the polluter pay the hidden cost, uphold labour rights. Both columns totalled honestly, then the fixes named.
